title: What is an anemic domain model and why is it criticized?
description: The difference between data-holder entities and real domain objects, why anemic models push rules into services, and when a plain data model is perfectly fine.

data.text: **Question:** What is an anemic domain model and why is it criticized?

An anemic domain model is an object model where entities are just data bags — public getters/setters with all business rules living in separate procedural service classes. It's criticized because it forfeits the main benefit of OOP: putting the data and the invariants that protect it in the same place. With an anemic model, any code can set `order.Status = Shipped` without payment, validation rules scatter across services, and the same rule gets reimplemented in several places. The counterpoint: not every project needs a rich domain model — for CRUD-shaped apps, anemic DTOs plus explicit service logic is simple and honest.

**Anemic (procedural style):**
- Entities: `{ get; set; }` properties only — no behavior
- `OrderService.PlaceOrder()`, `OrderService.CancelOrder()`, `PaymentService.MarkPaid()` each open the entity, check rules, and mutate properties
- Invariants ("can't ship unpaid", "can't cancel a delivered order") exist only as `if` statements scattered across services — nothing stops a new service from skipping them

**Rich domain model (OOP style):**
- `order.MarkPaid(paymentRef)` — only the object that owns the state can change it, and it validates its own invariants
- Illegal states are unrepresentable: no public setter, so "shipped but unpaid" can't be constructed
- Services orchestrate; entities decide. `OrderService` asks the order to do things; it doesn't do things *to* it

**Why teams still end up anemic:** ORMs like EF Core map nicely onto property bags (that's a legitimate influence), time pressure pushes logic into "just one more service class", and developers trained on CRUD-centric patterns reach for services by reflex. The cost accumulates: rule duplication, invariant violations discovered in production, and tests that must set up ten service calls to exercise one rule.

**The pragmatic line:**
- **Rich model where rules are complex and valuable**: orders, payments, bookings, state machines — invariants here prevent real money/consistency problems
- **Anemic is fine for**: DTOs, view models, config objects, simple CRUD with no cross-field rules, and data transfer across service boundaries (anemic is *correct* for a DTO — it's a packet, not a domain concept)
- A good heuristic: if you write `if (x.Status == ...)` checks in more than one service, that logic belongs on `x` itself

data.title: Anemic vs rich order model
Don't swing to the opposite extreme
data.text: A rich domain model doesn't mean every entity gets 40 methods, or that persistence and domain classes must be the same type. Many teams map an anemic persistence model to a rich domain model at the boundary — entities stay clean, ORM quirks stay in the repository layer. The point is where the *rules* live, not where the properties are.

Interviewers want to hear:
- A clear definition: data bags + service-layer rules vs behavior-owning entities
- The real cost: duplicated rules and unenforceable invariants
- That you're not dogmatic — CRUD apps legitimately stay anemic; rich models pay off where rules are complex
- A migration instinct: move each repeated status-check into the entity as a behavior

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Anemic model: entities are data bags, rules live in scattered services
Cost: duplicated rules, unenforceable invariants, easy illegal states
Rich model: objects own state changes and validate their own transitions
Not a universal rule — CRUD/DTOs legitimately stay anemic
data.takeaway: Put each business rule where its data lives: if three services re-check the same status, the status check belongs on the object itself.
